ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Reforms in Orissa Jails 
#*21.  SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA:† 
    SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that cash-starved state of Orissa has not 
been able to carry out the desired reforms in their jails; and 
(b) whether the Central Government propose to render financial or other 
help to overcome this handicap; if so, the details thereof, if not the reasons 
therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I. D. SWAM I): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Prison reforms is a continuous process and the Government 
of Orissa has been constructing additional prison wards to reduce the 
overcrowding and improve hygiene and sanitation in prisons in i phased manner. 
In order to supplement the efforts of the State oovernments to improve the 
condition of prisons, Central Government has been providing financial 
assistance to them under the scheme of the modernization of prison 
administration. During 1993-94 to 2001-02 the Government of Orissa was 
provided an amount of Rs. 233.78 lakhs under 
# Question No. 21 and 28 were taken together. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri

RAJYA SABHA [19 February, 2003] 
the scheme. Central Government has now launched a new non-plan scheme from the 
current financial year for construction of additional jails to reduce overcrowiding, 
repair and renovation of existing jails, improvement in sanitation and water 
supply and living accommodation for prison staff to be implemented over a 
period of five years with an outlay of Rs. 1800 crore on cost sharing basis in the 
ratio of 75:25 by the Central Government and the State Governments 
respectively. The tentative allocation under this scheme for Orissa for the next 
five years is Rs. 107.40 crore including the State share.

(c) The Government of Orissa has been alive to the needs of Prison Reforms 
which is a continuous process. They have been constructing additional prison wards to 
reduce the over crowding and improve hygiene and sanitation in prisons in a phased 
manner. In order to supplement the efforts of the State Government, the Central 
Government has been providing financial assistance to them under the Scheme 
of the Modernization of Prison Administration. During 1993-94 to 2001 -2002 the 
Government of Orissa was provided with an amount of Rs. 233.78 lakhs under the 
scheme. The Central Government has now launched a new non-plan scheme from the 
current financial year for this purpose. An amount of Rs. 107.40 crore including 25% 
State contribution is the proposed expenditure for Orissa, for the next five years 
under the scheme of Modernisation of Prisons.

Minister, the Orissa Government was given Rs. 233.78 lakhs between 1993-94 and 2001

the jails.which is required to be done by the Orissa Government. Now the Government 
proposes to give Rs. 107.40 crores. So, I want to know whether the Orissa Government 
has given any action plan as to how much money they ask for, to which

the whole country and, of course, for Orissa also, the amount has been already 
earmarked and they have made provisions. They have sent an action plan for

wards in all the sub-jails and also in district jails. The Action Plan has been put

that amount would be given every year, as per the Five-year Plan. In addition to 
that, theTenth Finance Commission and the Eleventh Finance Commission had 
also recommended certain amount for jail reforms and that has also been 
given to the States.

fast track courts which have been set up by the Government could be able to 
decide these cases so that the number of under-trials is reduced. 
SHRI I. D. SWAMI: Sir, there is no doubt that 75 per cent of the 
inmates in the jails are under-trails, and, for that, the Central Government, on its 
own, has been writing to the State Governments to form committees in which the 
officers of the prisons, officers of the district administration and officers of the 
district judiciary are involved, so that they can pay more frequent visits to the 
jails and dispose of certain cases.This has been done by some of the States. 
Andtthere is no doubt about it. In addition to that, so far as the question 
regarding reduction in number of under-trials is concerned, I would like to say that 
the directions or advisories have been sent to the State Governments. As the subject 
of prison reforms is that of the State Government, we have written to them that 
so far as the minor offences are concerned, the courts may be held in the prison 
premises, and those cases may be disposed of there itself. Sir, two 
Committees, namely, the Mullah Committee and the Kapur Committee were 
constituted on this subject.Those Committees had also recommended

Dialogue with Elected Representatives to Resolve Kashmir Issue 
*22. DR. KARAN SINGH: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Union Government is of the view that there is need for a 
dialogue with the elected representatives and the separatist groups to resolve 
the Kashmir issue; 
(b) if so, whether any steps have been taken or being taken in this regard; 
and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER, INCHARGE OFTHE MINISTRY 
OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L. K. ADVANI): (a) to (c) The Prime Minister in 
his address to the nation from the ramparts of Red Fort on August 15,2002 
had announced the resolve of the present Government at the Centre to initiate 
a dialogue with the elected representatives and other organizations in the State. 
Besides, as a matter of policy the Government continues to keep its doors open 
for talks with any groups or sections within J and K who eschew the path of 
violence. 
DR. KARAN SINGH: Mr. Chairman has kindly allowed me to put this 
Question in the unavoidable absence of Shri Ghulam Nabi Azad. Sir, I am 
grateful to you for the courtesy in allowing me to put this question in the 
unavoidable absence of Shri Ghulam Nabi Azad. 
Sir, Jammu and Kashmir has had a troubled history since 1947; I do not 
have to repeat that. The last 13 years of aggressive militancy have been full of 
disaster, destruction and death. Sir, the elections in September-October, 2002 
provided a new window of opportunity.The Prime Minister made a commitment 
from the ramparts of the Red Fort, which the hon. Minister has mentioned, that 
they would initiate dialogue with the elected representatives of the people and 
other organisations. Four-and-a-half months have elapsed since those 
elections but there seems to be no move yet, as far as we are aware, of initiating 
this important set of dialogue. 
5

Would the hon. Minister be pleased to state whether the Government is resiling 
from its publicly proclaimed position that they are going to initiate a dialogue with the

SHRI L. K. ADVANI: Sir, there is no question of the Government resiling

Government has decided to nominate Shri N. N. Vohra, former Home Secretary of 
the Government of India to cany on with these consultations. I have discussed the 
matter even with the Chief Minister, who has welcomed the proposal. How and 
when the whole process would start, would depend upon Mr. Vohra's discussions with 
the people concerned. 
DR. KARAN SINGH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, this is news to us that a new 
person has been nominated. There have been several people earlier who were called

SHRI L. K. ADVANI: I agree that process should be expedited. All that I can

Statement 
(a) and (b) During last year (2002) 671 communal incidents have been

Guidelines to promote Communal Harmony have also been issued to all the 
States/Union Territories.

been taking promotional efforts like observance of the Annual Quami Ekta Week, 
conferment of Awards like Communal Harmony Awards and Kabir Puraskar and 
allotment of grants to Non-Governmental Organisations who are engaged in 
various programmes.for the promotion of communal harmony in the country.The 
National Foundation for Communal Harmony, an autonomous organisation 
under the Union Home Ministry is also engaged in various programmes for the 
promotion of Communal Harmony in the country.

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) 
to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c)The 15th Electric Power Survey estimated demand in the 
country. It was on the basis of 16th Electric Power Survey that the Working Group 
on Power for the 10th Plan constituted by the Planning Commission estimated the 
need based requirement of capacity addition of 55,158 MW for the 10th Plan. 
After discussions with the State Utilities and the Central Undertakings, it 
recommended a feasible capacity addition of 46,939 MW. The matter was further 
deliberated with the Planning Commission and depending upon the availability 
of resources and readiness of the projects a capacity addition target of 41,110 MW 
was settled. Effective mechanisms have been put in place to ensure timely 
completion of the projects and achievement of the targetted capacity during 
10th Plan. 
In addition to the benefits from new generating capacity, the power 
supply position is expected to further improve through: 
An additional capacity of 3000 MW is expected to come from  
renewable sources of energy. In addition, supply of 1000 MW 
from Tala Hydroelectric Project in Bhutan is expected in the 
10th Plan. 
Undertaking energy conservation measures for which the 
Energy Conservation Act has been enacted and the Bureau of 
Energy Efficiency constituted. 
Reducing technical losses in distribution.The Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) is designed 
for the attainment of this objective. 
Undertaking Renovation Modernisation (R and M) of existing 
power stations which combined with improved Operation and 
Maintenance practices would lead to higher availability and 
generation. 
Export of power from surplus to deficit region through the gradual 
development of a National Grid to optimize utilization of 
generating capacity on an all India basis. 
Installation of capacity generating plants. The new Electricity 
Bill provides for a liberal framework for construction of 
captive power plants freely.

Under this initiative, the Gram Sabha would replace the Watershed

adequate technical expertise and experience would be identified to act as the 
PIA.This initiative is applicable to all new watershed development projects to be 
sanctioned in future.

Lower import tariffs on textiles products 
179. SHRI RUMANDLA RAAMACHANDRAYYA: Will the Minister of 
TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the India cotton textiles industry, especially the spinning 
segments, is seeking improved market access before it concedes to pressures 
for lower import tariffs on textiles products; 
(b) if so, whether industry representatives were involved in the high level 
meetings of the groups formed to suggest steps relating to market access 
negotiations with respect to textile items; 
(c) whether the Union Government has accepted the suggestions of the 
industry representatives which seeks greater market access; and 
(d) if so, the steps and assistance being provided to the textile 
industry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI BASANGOUDA R.  PATIL): (a) to (c) Tariff negotiations on non-
agricultural products, including textiles, has commenced in the World Trade 
Organisation (WTO) following the Doha Ministerial Declaration. The 
objective of the negotiations is improvement in market access, in particular on 
products of export interest to developing countries. Further, developing countries 
are expected to offer less than full reciprocity in reduction commitments. 
The Textile Commissioner had constituted two Industry Groups for 
making recommendations on market access negotiations for textile items. The 
Industry Groups which included, representatives from Cotton Textile Industry, 
had made recommendations to the effect that reduction of import duties for textile 
products in India should be proposed provided there was more than comparable 
reduction in the import duties of our major importing countries, our competing 
countries effected similar reductions and Government took necessary decisions 
for improving the competitiveness of Indian textile industry. 
122 

[19 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
At this stage the modalities for the negotiations are being discussed in the 
WTO and once the modalities are finalised the actual tariff negotiations would begin. 
India has submitted its proposals on modalities to the WTO on 30th December, 
2002 after holding inter-ministerial discussions and consultations with other 
stakeholders. 
(d) Government have been taking several steps from time to time to 
strengthen the textile industry. Some of the important initiatives are: 
(i) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
upgradation of the sector. 
(ii) Weaving, processing and garment machinery, which are covered under 
TUFS, have been extended the facility of accelerated depreciation at 
the rate of 50%. Cost of machinery has also been reduced through Fiscal 
Policy measures.This further encourages modernisation. 
(iii) Technology Mission of Cotton has been launched for initiating 
focussed steps for boosting production, productivity and quality of 
cotton for manufacture and export of competitive downstream textile 
products. 
(iv) With a view to encouraging backward integration, the custom duty 
on shuttleless looms has been brought from 15% to 5%. 
(v) National Institute for Fashion Technology (NIFT), its six branches and 
Apparel Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are running various 
courses/programmes to meet skilled manpower requirements of textile 
industry especially apparel in the field of design, merchandising and 
marketing. 
(vi) Facilities by way of eco-testing laboratories have been created to enable 
exporters to get the textile products pre-tested for conforming to the 
requirements of importing countries. 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [19 February, 2003] 
(vii) For upgrading infractructure facilities at important textile centres, a 
scheme Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme (TCIDS) 
has been launched.

SHRI LALITBHAI MEHTA (Gujarat) : Sir, the cattle population of the

one kg. of dung, total production would be 449.49 crore MT of compost 
organic manure per year. At present, the cultivable land in the country is put at

hectare of land, the need would be only 150 crore MT of compost organic 
manure. This would eliminate the use of chemical fertilizers, insecticides and 
pesticides and save valuable foreign exchange. This would also preserve the 
fertility of the land and give better quality of agricultural products, fruits and 
vegetables.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, hon. Members have expressed their apprehensions about the 
repealing of this Act. I want to bring to your kind notice that this Commission 
was constituted in 1984. It has not been operational for the past 4-5 years. In 
the year 1985, Banking Service Recruitment Boards were established for 
recruitment of officers and clerks in the nationalised banks. After that the State 
Bank of India and its associate banks have been recruiting their officers 
through their Regional Recruitment Boards. It was again reviewed in 1987. 
After the review, it was found that the Banking Sen/ice Recruitment Boards 
were doing well. They are, certainly, doing their recruitment well. Hence, it is 
not necessary to have the Banking Service Commission Act, which is not 
being implemented. After that, the Financial Systems Committee, I mean, the 
Narasimhan Committee, recommended the recruitment policy and said that it 
was not necessary to keep it in the Statute Book. After that a Committee, 
under the Chairmanship of Dr. D.R. Mehta, Deputy Governor of Reserve Bank, 
recommended the repeal of the Banking Service Commission Act, 1984. After 
that, because of various reasons, we felt that it should be repealed. During 
2001-02, while presenting the Budget, the hon. Finance Minister said that 
since autonomy was given to the banks to recruit the personnel according to 
their needs, the RRBs and the BSRBs should be abolished and that the 
selection 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [19 February, 2003] 
process should be handed over to the respective banks. It was only after that it 
was abolished. So, this Service Commission Act is not necessary to be kept in 
the Statute Book. Hence, we have brought this repeal Bill. At the same time, 
some hon. Members wanted to know, if it is abolished, what is the alternative 
to the Reservation Policy. Hon. Members, Shri Shunmugasundaram, Shri 
Viduthalai Virumbi and Shri Lalu Prasad, have stated that it is an anti-Dalit and 
anti-poor Government. It is not like that. We are for the development and 
welfare of the poor people. We are adhering to our Reservation Policy and 
instructing the banks that, while recruiting officers of Class-I or Class-ll or 
Groups C & D employees, they should adhere to the Reservation Policy. The 
respective Bank Boards are given the power. They will adhere to the 
Reservation Policy in respect of SCs, STs and OBCs. They will do their 
recruitment, according to the Reservation Policy. If anybody fails in this 
respect, the Government will intervene and take necessary action and those 
who are responsible will be punished. I assure this House that the Reservation 
Policy would continue and it will be adhered to at all levels including Group-C 
arid Group-D. With these words, I request the whole House to approve this 
repeal Bill.

THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Dr. Prabha Thakur.   She is not present. 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karnataka): Madam, it is very 
unfortunate that our country has to face a severe drought. Drought is a 
recurring phenomenon. Every year, a few States are affected by drought. 
Millions of farmers suffer because of that. They not only incur losses but also 
suffer a lot. Factors like their crop failure, economic losses and their inability to 
pay debt are forcing them to end their life. The trend shows suicide by farmers 
is rising. Every day, we read in newspapers about the farmer committing 
suicide for his inability to pay the loans he had taken for agriculture. In an 
agriculture predominant country, this should not happen. We have to find out 
both long-term and short-term solutions to the problem of drought in our 
country. 
Short-term solutions can include a better management of the existing 
water resources, crop planning rotation, proper guidance to farmers by the 
State Government and waiver of loans to farmers. The small and marginal 
farmers should be given due importance. They should be given financial 
assistance to withstand the drought conditions. They can be engaged in 
alternative jobs to help them economically. 
So far as long-term measures are concerned, linking of rivers, proper 
crop planning etc. are the solutions. The Government has initiated action on 
linking of rivers. This is a welcome step. Now, it is to be seen how the 
Government moves on this project. Let it not remain only on paper. 
The Government has also provided financial relief to the farmers in 
order to compensate them for the losses suffered in unirrigated areas in the 
form of a special Drought Relief Price ranging from Rs.5/- to Rs.20/- per 
quintal. This is inadequate. It should be raised to appropriately compensate 
the farmers. The States should also ensure a timely flow of institutional credit 
to the farmers. 
I am sorry to point out that the Central Government has not provided 
enough financial aid to the States. Against the demand for Rs. 1,562 crores 
made by the Karnataka Government, the Central Government has provided 
only Rs.221 crores. For Madhya Pradesh, against its demand for Rs.790 
crores, only Rs. 126 crores have been provided, and for Rajasthan, against its 
demand for Rs.7,519 crores, only Rs.207 crores have been provided. In total, 
as against the demand for Rs.31,102 cores, only Rs. 1,999 crores have been 
provided. 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [19 February, 2003] 
As per a study, the spectre of drought over a vast area of India could 
cost the Exchequer over Rs.1,000 crores. This means, allocation for 
development will be either reduced or diverted to the relief and rehabilitation 
schemes. 
There is a need to solve the inter-State water disputes amicably and 
in a harmonious manner so as to ensure an equitable availability of water 
during dry spells. In Karnataka, 186 taluks have been declared as drought-hit 
areas. The amount released to Karnataka is very meagre. Our hon. Chief 
Minister made repeated requests for extra foodgrains for "food for work" 
programme. But nothing has been done so far. I request the hon. Minister to 
release extra foodgrains to Karnataka as early as possible. It is also important 
to work out a viable water management system, in view of the unprecedented 
drought faced by the 14 States during the last year. Indian farmers are very 
hard working, but weather is not helping them. Drought and untimely rains 
frustrate their efforts. That makes them commit suicide. The worst sufferers are 
the small and marginal farmers and landless labourers. Government should 
ensure that these categories of farmers are not affected and they are properly 
compensated. Our hon. President, Madam Sonia Gandhi, has requested our 
hon. Prime Minister to make known in advance the entire allocation that could 
be given to each State, at least as a projection. So, our hon. Prime Minister 
should have taken that suggestion and made a note in advance to the States 
on the allocation they are giving to each State, and also released at least 50 
per cent of the capital initially so that the State can ensure an uninterrupted 
flow of foodgrains in the affected areas. Madam Sonia Gandhi also requested 
for delegation of powers to the Central Relief Commissioner to respond 
immediately to the distress signals from the State. Madam, unless you 
delegate the powers to Central Relief Commissioner, he cannot immediately 
respond, and he has to take long time because of the long process and the 
paper work, which takes long time. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY) in the Chair] 
So, it will affect the persons more and more.   I hope the hon. Minister will take 
these suggestions and help the people of our country.
